issues.what: 'Their shapes grew inside the mountain's rock' is the old formative-force idea told honestly, but the stem has already called them 'fossils of crinoids', and T1 rock-layers-and-fossils taught that a fossil is what a living thing left, so it is barely live. The sea-rose lure (T1's own 'an ocean once covered it', pushed too far) is strong, and the question goes a grade past T1.
issues.fix: Acceptable as a respectable wrong theory of the past. If a livelier lure is wanted: 'Seabirds carried them up and dropped them'.

issues.what: Three wrong choices are one kind (wind, birds or currents carried its seeds) and the key is the only one of another kind, so the odd one out wins; the stem's 'Today wide oceans part those lands' also hints that it was not always so.
issues.fix: Drop 'Today': 'Wide oceans lie between those lands.' Replace 'Winds blew its seeds from land to land' with the honest alternative a student might reach for: choices 'The lands were once joined together', 'The plant arose on each land by itself', 'Birds carried its seeds from land to land', 'Sea currents floated its seeds to each land'.

issues.what: Every choice carries its own answer: 'roamed the open ocean', 'flew far over the sea' and 'tiny spores rode the wind' each say how that creature crosses an ocean, and the key says 'lived only on dry land'. A student who knows nothing of fossils or moving continents picks it by reading the choices; the question tests no fact.
issues.fix: Strip the crossing cues and make the choices parallel, so the student must know which can cross: 'Geologists find fossils of one kind of living thing on two coasts that face each other across an ocean. Fossils of which of these would give the strongest evidence that the two lands were once joined?' Choices: 'A plant-eating reptile as big as a pig', 'A shark as long as a rowing boat', 'A seabird as big as a goose', 'A tree fern as tall as a house'. The fern is the lure that needs knowledge (fern spores ride the wind across oceans, F11, and Glossopteris, the unit's star evidence, was a seed fern). The context's Lystrosaurus and Mesosaurus stay.

issues.what: 'Thick ice covered it, much as it does now' is the no-change choice in a question that asks what the coal shows about long ago; a careful player strikes it at once, leaving three.
issues.fix: Replace it with a real mix-up about black rock: 'Volcanoes poured black lava across it'.

issues.what: The key rests on T1's fact that coal comes from buried swamp plants (rock-layers-and-fossils teaches it in its oil question's lure and context); the T3 part, that a now-frozen land once had a mild, wet climate, is a short step past it. Acceptable for the evidence the lead gave this unit, and it keeps clear of the equator half-truth (F14).

Two wrong choices are weak: 'They rose apart and came out alike by chance' cannot stand against the stem's 'the same kinds of rock, formed at the same time and folded in the same way', and 'Glaciers dragged rock from one to the other' across an ocean, mountains and all, is not live. Only Werner's worldwide sea competes with the key.
issues.fix: Use respectable wrong ideas: choices 'They formed as one range that later split', 'A shrinking Earth wrinkled both at once' (the contracting Earth, F23 of plates-at-work), 'One worldwide sea laid the same rock in both', 'The same kind of magma rose under both'.

issues.what: The stem lists the layers bottom first ('At the bottom ... in the middle ... and on top ...'), so the key just reads the stem's order back: a student who knows nothing of superposition maps the list straight onto 'from first to last'. The top-down misconception lure only works on a student who reverses the stem, which no one does by accident.
issues.fix: List them top first: 'A cliff shows three flat, unbroken layers of rock. On top lies sandstone made from the sand of desert dunes, in the middle a seam of coal, and at the bottom limestone packed with seashells. What was this spot, from first to last?' Same choices; now the naive reading lands on the lure 'Desert, then swamp forest, then sea'.

issues.what: 'They settled on end, just as they stand now' is weak: sand and mud settling as a vertical wall is not a picture any student holds (the steep-slope choice carries the real mix-up).
issues.fix: 'Ice in their cracks pushed them upright' (frost wedging, taught in T1, misapplied).

issues.what: The stem says the crack 'runs through all six', and the key repeats 'all six'. With the two 'while ... forming' choices dead (a crack that breaks the top layer cannot have formed while a lower one was being laid), it is a two-way choice that plain logic settles without the cross-cutting idea.
issues.fix: Make it need superposition and cross-cutting together: 'A road cut through a hill shows six flat layers of rock. A crack, called a fault, runs up through the bottom four, which have slipped a metre lower on one side of it, but the top two layers lie unbroken across it. When did the fault form?' Choices: 'After the bottom four, before the top two', 'After all six layers had formed', 'Before any of the six layers formed', 'While the bottom layer was forming'.

issues.what: The three wrong conditions (the thickest bottom layer, the most fossils, one colour) have nothing to do with order, and no student thinks a geologist must check them before trusting the rule; the key is the only choice about the stack's order, so it wins by elimination.
issues.fix: Use conditions a student might really think the rule needs, which it does not: choices 'That the layers have not been flipped over', 'That no layer has been worn away by erosion', 'That every layer formed under the sea', 'That the layers are all of one kind of rock'. (A gap worn by erosion leaves the lower layers still older, and superposition holds for layers laid on land as well as in the sea.)

unit_notes: Ownership clean under the lead's 2026-11-26 ruling: nothing keys Wegener, the jigsaw fit, Pangaea, the land-bridge critics, Steno, index fossils or an age in years. fb3f578248 (a fault is younger than the layers it cuts) is relative dating, which reading-deep-time owns as a concept, but it is the lead's 'broken after they formed', so it stays here. Lanes clean: Everest, Antarctica, and the Appalachians with Scotland and Norway set the scene, and each stem states what the key needs (the height, the ice, the Atlantic between them); no key is a place. Crinoids, Glossopteris, Lystrosaurus and Mesosaurus serve as evidence, not as animal facts. Against T1 rock-layers-and-fossils: 7dda748841 goes a grade deeper (T1's 'An ocean once covered it' is now its lure); 65d31b180e leans on T1's coal fact (see its note); no T1 question asked oldest-at-the-bottom, so 4c309d00f8 and a51b4b684c are new. Against plates-at-work: 7dda748841 says only that old sea floor was pushed up, and plates-at-work's 20b877c08a keys the collision itself; no clash. Within the unit: 43c0731f4f and a44c1dd82e both key 'the lands were once joined' (once from fossils, once from mountains), and 23736dfd81 asks which fossil shows the same; three evidence questions with one conclusion is what the lead assigned, but once a player has seen one the others' keys are expected, so their distractor fixes matter more. a51b4b684c's stem states superposition ('usually takes the bottom layer to be the oldest'), which gives 4c309d00f8's rule to anyone who meets it first; the top-first fix on 4c309d00f8 still makes the player apply it.
